payload.author: Biswa96
payload.body: I'm not sure if the issue should be fixed with this change. 3.5.30.1 tag is present in upstream repository https://sourceforge.net/p/djvu/djvulibre-git/ci/release.3.5.30.1/tree/

payload.author: GourangaDasSamrat
payload.body:
@Biswa96 You're right that the `release.3.5.30.1` tag exists — I checked it.

 But note that this is a tag in the **`djvulibre-git`** source-control repo, which is a separate tool from the **Files** section of the same SourceForge project. `TERMUX_PKG_SRCURL` downloads a packaged tarball from `Files/DjVuLibre/`, not from the git repo — and the latest tarball actually published there is still 3.5.30.

 Also interesting: the commit that `release.3.5.30.1` points to (`af7431`) has the commit message *"properly tag release 3.5.30 (in ddjvuapi.pc for...)"* — so even upstream's own commit message calls it "3.5.30", not "3.5.30.1". It looks like the `.1` tag naming convention doesn't correspond to an actual packaged release.

 So there's no tarball for repology's "3.5.30.1" to download, which is why auto-update was failing. This PR's regexp constrains the updater to plain `X.Y.Z` versions so it stops trying to fetch versions that only exist as git tags, not as tarball releases. Once upstream actually publishes a 3.5.30.1 (or newer) tarball in the Files section, this regexp will match it fine and auto-update will resume normally.

 Alternatively, if you'd prefer, we could switch `TERMUX_PKG_SRCURL` to pull from the git repo/tag directly instead of the tarball release — happy to do that if that's the preferred direction, just let me know.

payload.author: flipphoneguy
payload.body:
Okay I did some more static and dynamic analysis and I'm pretty sure I've figured it out. It's a race! I'm not sure if you had the time or patience to look at the upstream code so I'll try to explain it without naming the src files and functions. If you are looking at the code lmk and I'll point you to my findings.

The process of shutting down safely with liburcu qsbr goes something like this: when a worker finishes its work it does a check to ensure no other process is online/awake, to assert that no one's in middle of trying to write another task to its queue while it dies. Once there are no other busy workers, it heads to a point where it just waits till all processes get there and then they are safely killed.

The bug is that when a worker gets to the final gate, it doesn't mark itself offline (unlike other points in the same source file). Therefore, when 1 worker is at the gate and a second worker performs the check, it'll hang indefinitely because the first worker is still online. 

The race (or the case it doesn't hang) is that if 2 workers arrive at the check at the same time (or the second one will arrive there while the first one is still in middle of performing the check), one of them will just sleep and wait for the check to complete, and once the first worker finishes the check, the second queued worker just skips straight to the gate. And since there are only 2 workers in dig, if all jobs they had to do finished at the same time, then it won't hang. 

But again, the race isn't the bug. It's just a scenario in which the buggy code doesn't fail. The patch is still accurate. 

This might explain why the first time you tried on your Android device, you couldn't reproduce (although by me it reproduced every single time. But that's the nature of a race. They'll never be the same on 2 devices).

TLDR

I realized this became pretty lengthy as I was writing. In short, there's a race that will determine whether the case where the bug is present is triggered and it hangs indefinitely or not. That's why it worked for you on a Linux machine. This patch fixes the bug altogether (which on my Android devices at least the bug is triggered every time)

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
> Inside node_modules/sharp/dist/libvips.cjs, pkgConfigPath() runs pkg-config --variable pc_path pkg-config (getPkgConfigPath()), which on the host Ubuntu builder evaluates to:
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pkgconfig:/usr/share/pkgconfig:/usr/lib/pkgconfig

It is unfortunate that this command does indeed give the Ubuntu pkg-config folders, even though the wrapper is used:

```
builder@bc74c84f6e1e:~/termux-packages$ ~/.termux-build/_cache/android-r29-api-24-v4/bin/pkg-config --variable pc_path pkg-config
/usr/local/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pkgconfig:/usr/local/lib/pkgconfig:/usr/local/share/pkgconfig:/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pkgconfig:/usr/lib/pkgconfig:/usr/share/pkgconfig
builder@bc74c84f6e1e:~/termux-packages$ 
```

I wish that the wrapper could somehow resolve this, but unfortunately it might not be possible without either going back to building a custom `pkgconf` package, or attempting to parse and hook the arguments to `pkg-config` in the wrapper, which can turn into a mess. I think patching this package is fine because no or few other packages use this specific `pkg-config` command.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
We don't generally package fonts in the repositories unless they are required for specific packages.

`ttf-dejavu` is used by `fontconfig` and `gtk{2,3,4}`.
`ttf-jetbrains-mono` and `ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols` are used by `wezterm`.

Font packages tend to be very large and are architecture independent.
The Iosevka font family for example is 382MiB in ZIP form and over 1.1GiB decompressed.
###### see: https://archlinux.org/packages/extra/any/ttf-iosevka-nerd/

Font selection is up to user preference and I think we should leave it up to the user to decide which fonts they want to install.
Providing them in the repos has very marginal benefits and would consume significant amounts of space on the repos.

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
Since the preexisting nerd-fonts package in Termux, `ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols`, uses the same name as Arch Linux's package for the same thing, could you please use the Arch Linux naming convention for all of these other nerd-fonts packages?

https://archlinux.org/groups/any/nerd-fonts/

payload.author: GourangaDasSamrat
payload.body:
Thanks for the feedback @TomJo2000!

@robertkirkman - done, renamed all packages to follow the Arch Linux nerd-fonts naming convention (`ttf-<font>-nerd`), pushed above.

@TomJo2000 - I understand the concern about repo size, but I'd like to make the case for keeping these:

- Both Homebrew (`brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font`, etc.) and Arch Linux (69 individual `ttf-*-nerd` packages in `extra`) ship every Nerd Font as a separate, opt-in package - this is the standard approach across package managers, not an Arch-only convention.
- These are purely opt-in: nothing in the base system or any other package depends on them. A user who doesn't want a Nerd Font simply never runs `pkg install ttf-<font>-nerd`, so there's zero cost to anyone who doesn't install them.
- Repo storage isn't duplicated per-install - each package is only downloaded once, by the user who explicitly chose it, same as any other optional package already in the repo.
- `ttf-jetbrains-mono` and `ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols` already established this exact pattern; Nerd Fonts are extremely commonly requested by Termux users for shell prompts (Powerlevel10k, Starship) and icon-aware tools (lsd, eza, nvim file trees) - having them installable via `pkg install` (instead of everyone manually curl/unzip-ing from GitHub releases into `~/.termux/font.ttf`) is a meaningful quality-of-life improvement, not just a "nice to have."

If repo size for the largest fonts (Iosevka, Meslo with 24 style variants) is still a concern, I'm happy to trim the style set further per package, or drop the largest ones and keep only the small/medium ones. Let me know what would work.

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
> Both Homebrew (brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font, etc.) and Arch Linux (69 individual ttf-*-nerd packages in extra) ship every Nerd Font as a separate, opt-in package - this is the standard approach across package managers, not an Arch-only convention.

When it comes to number of packages and packaging policy, Termux is different from other repositories because Termux has only a little more than 3000 packages. Both Homebrew and Arch Linux as well as most other desktop Linux and Mac repositories have well over 10000 packages. in Termux we focus on providing and maintaining packages that are otherwise not convenient for people to install quickly on Android and which do not consist primarily of niche, static cosmetic assets that never require patching to work directly copied and pasted into Termux, like wallpapers, fonts, themes and icon packs. That being said, these fonts do have a high repology score. https://repology.org/project/fonts%3Anerd-fonts/versions Let's add them if at least one other person asks for packages of these; there is currently no package request for more of the nerd fonts.

Closing this for now — the from-source Android build turned out to require more than I can commit to right now: a strictly pinned LLVM 21.1.8, pinned Rust nightly, NDK cross-toolchain setup, and a static cross-compiled ICU for Android whose build recipe I couldn't locate anywhere public (checked `oven-sh/bun`, `oven-sh/bun-development-docker-image`, and the actual `.buildkite/Dockerfile` — the `webkit.ts` comment pointing to a "Dockerfile.android" recipe doesn't seem to correspond to anything I could find).

Summary of what I confirmed, in case anyone picks this up later:
- Bun's build system has official Android cross-compile support (`--abi=android`, `--android-ndk=<path>`), pattern confirmed in `.buildkite/Dockerfile` (NDK r27c, host-clang + sysroot).
- WebKit doesn't need to be built from source for Android — a prebuilt tarball is fetched automatically.
- The remaining blocker is a static, cross-built ICU (`$BUN_ANDROID_ICU_ROOT`) that I couldn't find a public recipe for.

Thanks for the guidance along the way, @robertkirkman — apologies I couldn't land this one. Will revisit if upstream's Android/ICU story becomes clearer.

payload.body: Yes — I used LLM/AI assistance while developing and debugging this package and while drafting parts of the PR. I should have disclosed that up front; apologies. I have been validating the resulting changes with actual source builds, package inspection, and native Termux runtime tests rather than treating generated code as sufficient. I’ll adapt the recipe to Termux’s packaging conventions based on this review, and I’m now working through the concrete architecture request by determining which Termux architectures workerd can actually build and run on before updating `TERMUX_PKG_EXCLUDED_ARCHES`. payload.author: adybag14-cyber
payload.body:
Thanks for the review. I reworked the package around the points raised rather than only explaining the existing form.

- **LLM assistance:** disclosed above. I used AI assistance for implementation/debugging and drafting, with the result validated using actual source builds and Termux runtime tests.
- **Architectures:** the recipe now supports both 64-bit Termux architectures, `aarch64` and `x86_64`. `arm` and `i686` remain excluded because the pinned workerd source explicitly says its Bazel zlib port does not support architectures other than x86_64/arm64, and its pinned Rust target/toolchain list is likewise 64-bit-only.
  - `x86_64`: the normal Termux package builder produced `wrangler_4.123.0_x86_64.deb` (50,012,248 bytes, SHA-256 `4ff5bf43d8ab3087dc272a34de256f158bce8ac9a9506beb9b62f6e07adf7b94`). In a Termux x86_64 userspace, Node reported `android:x64`, Wrangler `4.123.0`, workerd `2026-08-11`, esbuild `0.28.1`; `wrangler deploy --dry-run` passed and a real `wrangler dev` returned `termux-wrangler-x86-ok`.
  - `aarch64`: a forced rebuild of the same revised tree produced `wrangler_4.123.0_aarch64.deb` (46,499,908 bytes, SHA-256 `dfaa4c605306fcea17863f174028779c6bddce4a5695c68b03eb62c0592e58dc`). Android Node reported `android:arm64`, Wrangler `4.123.0`, workerd `2026-08-11`, esbuild `0.28.1`; `wrangler deploy --dry-run` passed and a real `wrangler dev` returned `termux-wrangler-arm64-ok`.
- **Endian code:** I removed the big-endian branch. The Android shim is now little-endian-only, matching the supported Termux targets. I also tested removing the Android endian shim entirely; workerd then reached final link and failed on undefined `htobe32`/`htobe64`, so the Android definitions are required by this port rather than speculative compatibility code.
- **Five esbuild versions:** these are not arbitrary. The filtered `wrangler...` pnpm install contains exactly esbuild `0.18.20`, `0.23.1`, `0.24.2`, `0.27.3`, and `0.28.1`, and exactly those five `@esbuild/linux-x64` executable payloads are present. Because install scripts are disabled and the package is source-only, the recipe source-builds those host executables before Wrangler's build runs. Only target esbuild `0.28.1` is installed in the final Termux package.
- **Install helper:** `prepare-wrangler-deploy.py` is custom Termux packaging glue, not an upstream build file. I moved its invocation into `termux_step_make_install()` so the package follows the normal Termux build/install phase separation. Its role is limited to making pnpm's deploy tree relocatable/self-contained, rejecting/removing foreign native npm payloads, pointing workerd at the source-built Android binary, and creating the launchers.
- **Manual test:** I moved the smoke test to `packages/wrangler/tests/smoke.sh`, following the existing `packages/ldc/tests/hello_world.sh` layout. It is not wired into external Termux CI.

The revised tree also passes `scripts/lint-packages.sh`, Bash/Python syntax checks, metadata/source closure, and a clean-tag dry-run of the workerd patch against `v1.20260811.1`.

payload.author: GourangaDasSamrat
payload.body:
@robertkirkman I tested the `libsqlite3.DLL.basename` override locally and both `sqlcipher` and `proton-pass-cli` build successfully with it.

Summary of the change (pushed on top of the earlier `TEMP` revision-bump commit): instead of installing as `libsqlite3.so.*` and then renaming the symlink chain in `post_massage` (which breaks the embedded symlink targets, since `mv` on a symlink only renames the link itself, not what it points to), I'm now overriding sqlite/sqlcipher's `main.mk` variable that controls the shared library's basename:

```bash
TERMUX_PKG_EXTRA_MAKE_ARGS="libsqlite3.DLL.basename=libsqlcipher"
```

`main.mk`'s own `install-dll-unix-generic` rule already correctly builds the versioned symlink chain at install time (`mv` on the real file, then `ln -s` with correct target names) — it just needed to be told to use `libsqlcipher` as the basename instead of the default `libsqlite3`. `TERMUX_PKG_EXTRA_MAKE_ARGS` is passed to both `make` and `make install`, so `libsqlcipher.so`/`.so.0`/`.so.<version>` are built and installed with the correct names from the start. No post-install symlink surgery needed at all, and `post_massage` is now much simpler.

Let me know if you'd like me to trigger the CI run here, or if you want to review/verify it yourself first.

I think so, but I wonder what you think about that. I was hoping to create a patch that could allow removing the entire `termux_step_post_massage()`, by also automatically doing that at the same point that the `.so` file is renamed, but such a patch might belong better upstream, because every other distro is also dealing with this problem.

payload.author: GourangaDasSamrat
payload.body:
@robertkirkman
> Why does this comment talk about a broken symlink chain?

You're right, that comment still had leftover wording from describing the old bug. The actual reason for this change is different — it's not fixing a broken chain (that's already fixed since #31010), it's avoiding the post-install rename step entirely by having the build produce the correct `libsqlcipher.so*` names from the start, which is simpler and has less surface area for future bugs like the one we just fixed. I'll update the comment to say that explicitly instead of referencing the old broken-chain issue.

> Would you describe the fact that libsqlite3.DLL.basename=libsqlcipher does not automatically rename the .pc file (and other files)... as an issue that should be reported upstream?

That makes sense to me. Looking at `main.mk`, the basename override only affects the shared library build/install rules — the `.pc` file, headers, and man page installs all reference `sqlite3`/`libsqlite3` independently, with no shared "rename everything for a forked project" mechanism. Since sqlcipher is explicitly a documented soft-fork use case (and presumably other distros hit the same issue, as you mentioned), a proper `--with-lib-basename=X` style option upstream that touches all of these consistently does sound like it'd be worth reporting. I'm happy to draft that upstream issue if you'd like, though I don't have deep familiarity with sqlite's autosetup/`auto.def` internals so I might need your input on how far it should go (e.g. should it also rename `sqlite3.h`, or just leave that to downstream since header renaming is more disruptive to API consumers).

> are you able to trigger the CI run here?

I just tried requesting a review, but the workflow still shows "awaiting approval" on my end — so it looks like I don't have permission to approve it myself, only a maintainer can. Sorry for the confusion earlier — the successful run I mentioned testing was on my own fork's branch (I ran the workflow there myself), not this PR directly. Let me know once you get a chance to approve the run here.

payload.author: GourangaDasSamrat
payload.body:
@robertkirkman On reflection, I don't think a broader "rename everything" upstream mechanism is realistic to ask for — the `.pc` file and man page are low-risk, but the headers and function names (`sqlite3_open()`, `#include <sqlite3.h>`, etc.) are part of the public API that a huge number of programs depend on. Giving that a build-time rename flag risks it being used accidentally and silently breaking ABI/API expectations across projects. That's presumably exactly why upstream only exposes the shared-library basename as overridable — it's safe because it only affects the linker-visible file name, not the actual symbols or headers a program includes.

So I think the current split is actually the right shape: `TERMUX_PKG_EXTRA_MAKE_ARGS` handles the one thing that's safe to override upstream (the `.so` basename), and the remaining `mv`/`sed` calls in `post_massage` for bin/headers/pkgconfig/man stay as-is, since those are Termux-specific packaging choices (avoiding file collisions with the `sqlite` package) rather than something upstream should bake in. I don't think there's a good upstream issue to file here after all — happy to be corrected if you see it differently.

payload.author: lesliechowsh
payload.body:
1) You're right — I missed it, thanks for catching that. `packages/nodejs-lts/build.sh` (Node 24.18.0 LTS) has the same configure invocation without `--use-prefix-to-find-headers`, and ships the same `common.gypi.patch`, so it needs the same change. Verified on-device: with the official downloaded headers node-gyp fails with `gyp: Undefined variable android_ndk_path in binding.gyp`; with the local patched headers the same module builds fine. Updating the PR to cover both — done, the branch now touches both packages.

2) Partially. #27724 configures npm at postinst — user-side setup; this PR fixes the root cause at build time. Two observations from checking the code and the package layout:
- With the flag, node-gyp's getNodeDir() (lib/configure.js) locates the headers at $PREFIX/include/node automatically, with zero user config. #27724's nodedir setting points at $PREFIX/lib/nodejs, which does not exist — Termux headers live in $PREFIX/include/node — so as written it wouldn't take effect.
- The python/cc/cxx/ar/strip presets and the missing-tools hint are independent and still useful.
So if this lands, I'd suggest #27724 drops the nodedir line (or points it at $PREFIX) and keeps the environment presets.

3) Any native module build that compiles from source — e.g. `node-gyp rebuild` in a package tree with a binding.gyp, like node-pty when built from source. node-gyp downloads the official headers (URL built in lib/process-release.js) because use_prefix_to_find_headers is off, then fails in configure:
```
gyp: Undefined variable android_ndk_path in binding.gyp while trying to load binding.gyp
gyp ERR! configure error
```
Reproduced on-device (aarch64, Node v26.4.0) on a minimal binding.gyp and on node-pty's own tree; with the local patched headers the same builds succeed. Note: plain `npm i node-pty` won't show it — the package ships prebuilt binaries and npm 12 blocks install scripts unless approved. Full repro steps in #30975.

payload.author: lesliechowsh
payload.body: Small correction to point 2 above: rather than claiming $PREFIX/lib/nodejs does not exist, the stronger argument is about what node-gyp does with nodedir — it looks for <nodedir>/include/node. The headers are installed at $PREFIX/include/node (make install with --prefix=$TERMUX_PREFIX, nothing in the package creates a lib/nodejs path), so `nodedir $PREFIX/lib/nodejs` points at a location that cannot contain the headers, and the setting would not take effect as written.

payload.author: lesliechowsh
payload.body: One more correction to point 3 above — I checked node-pty 1.1.0's prebuilds: they only cover darwin-x64/arm64 and win32-x64/arm64, no linux/android. So on Termux the install script's prebuild check fails and it falls back to `node-gyp rebuild`, which is exactly why `npm i node-pty` fails with the android_ndk_path error on current Termux (npm 11.x runs install scripts normally). My earlier note about prebuilt binaries only holds for macOS/Windows; the npm 12 script-blocking note applies only to users who upgraded to npm 12. The repro steps in #30975 are correct as written for current Termux.

payload.author: VaclavSynacek
payload.body:
Thanks for the review.

I applied the quoting and style suggestions, changed the links to use `ln -sf`, and inlined the single-use path variable.

I also tested both compiler overrides:

- a clean host bootstrap succeeds without explicitly passing `CC=gcc`
- the target build succeeds without explicitly passing `CC_FOR_BUILD=gcc`, using the value exported by Termux’s toolchain setup

Both overrides have therefore been removed.

I tested the proposed `TERMUX_PKG_EXTRA_CONFIGURE_ARGS` approach as well. Unfortunately, Chez uses a custom configure script rather than Autotools, while Termux’s standard configure step automatically supplies Autotools arguments. The build fails immediately with:

```text
option '--disable-dependency-tracking' unrecognized or missing an argument
```

Other automatically supplied options such as `--host`, `--libdir`, `--includedir`, and `--disable-rpath` are likewise not supported by Chez’s configure script. I have therefore retained the `termux_step_configure` override, while removing the redundant `CC_FOR_BUILD` argument from it.

The revised recipe passes a clean AArch64 build and a subsequent forced rebuild.

payload.author: VaclavSynacek
payload.body:
Thanks for testing the on-device build and reporting this.

I reproduced the missing iconv symbols on a physical AArch64 Termux device. The failure occurs in the host bootstrap during an on-device build: unlike glibc, Android does not provide iconv through libc. Passing `LIBS=-liconv` to the host configure step when `TERMUX_ON_DEVICE_BUILD=true` fixes both the portable-bytecode bootstrap executable and the native host executable.

A clean on-device build then exposed a second Android-specific issue during installation. Chez’s installer creates hardlinks for its executable and boot-file aliases, but Android rejects those hardlinks before `termux_step_post_make_install` can replace them. I added a small patch to Chez’s installer helper so these aliases are created directly as relative symlinks instead. This also allows the previous post-install hardlink conversion to be removed.

The following aliases are now installed as relative symlinks:

```text
chez-petite -> chez
scheme-script -> chez
chez.boot -> scheme.boot
chez-petite.boot -> petite.boot
scheme-script.boot -> scheme.boot
```

Validation performed with the revised recipe:

- clean Docker AArch64 build passes
- clean on-device AArch64 package build passes
- both host bootstrap link stages include `-liconv`
- package installation succeeds on Android
- all executable and boot aliases are relative symlinks
- `scheme-script` and `chez` run successfully from the on-device-built package
- `dpkg -V chez-scheme chez-scheme-static` passes

Regarding X11: the expression editor itself remains enabled. In current Chez, X11 is used only by the expression editor’s optional X primary-selection/clipboard integration. It dynamically opens `libX11`, but still requires X11 headers at build time. Disabling that optional integration avoids making a main-repository package depend on the separate X11 repository. I added a comment to the recipe clarifying this.

I also added a comment explaining why the custom `termux_step_configure` override is necessary: Chez’s configure script is not generated by GNU Autotools and rejects the extra Autotools options supplied by Termux’s standard configure step.

payload.author: serge-medvedev
payload.body:
Herdr does useful work without a coding agent: it is a standalone persistent terminal workspace manager. It creates ordinary shell panes, tabs, and workspaces, keeps their processes running across detach/reattach, and provides split, navigation, copy, and remote/session workflows. Agent detection and status reporting are optional additions; unsupported agents still run normally as terminal processes.

The agent I installed and validated on Termux was the `@mmmbuto/codex-cli-termux` npm package described above. Herdr 0.8.0 also recognizes agents including Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Kimi, Hermes Agent, Codex, and others, but none of those is currently an installable package in this repository's main package set. Adding `nodejs` as a recommendation would not install an agent, while recommending a third-party npm or TUR package from a main-repository package would not be an accurate package relationship.

Therefore `TERMUX_PKG_RECOMMENDS` is not appropriate here: Herdr is independently functional, and its optional agent integrations are installed separately by users who need them.

Check the default config (which is all commented out by default).

It is an oldie unix admin tool. Not a very compkex, but a very useful one.

Particular importance is coming from that these veteran unix admins have many decade experience to create the reachable stability in sometimes a bit braindead environment. That is the very same case as today the Google and the phone vendors let us sucking where they only can.

payload.author: 3ls-it
payload.body:
> > The upstream TiEmu 3.03 distribution includes legacy PedroM 0.81 .tib images, which are not accepted by the current TiEmu import path
> 
> I was wondering, is this problem currently reproducible in any desktop Linux distro package `tiemu`, or require any mitigations there, and if so, could you show which distro is affected and/or how it is mitigated on a desktop Linux distro?

payload.author: 3ls-it
payload.body: > > > The upstream TiEmu 3.03 distribution includes legacy PedroM 0.81 .tib images, which are not accepted by the current TiEmu import path > > > > > > I was wondering, is this problem currently reproducible in any desktop Linux distro package `tiemu`, or require any mitigations there, and if so, could you show which distro is affected and/or how it is mitigated on a desktop Linux distro? > > I'll look into that. Interesting results given the small sample size. I'm able to confirm that TiEmu on Ubuntu and FreeBSD both have the same issue of not being able to use the included images. The `.tib` images are included and are identical: ``` (ins)~/.../tiemu-3.03/pedrom $ sha256sum pedrom89.tib 4e04d4b53841aaf511934cf7a5fd4a9bb4603112f9b6fb9d577f69ac63e4d695 pedrom89.tib ``` ``` (ins)jfa@LinuxBuildHost:/usr/share/tiemu/pedrom$ sha256sum pedrom89.tib 4e04d4b53841aaf511934cf7a5fd4a9bb4603112f9b6fb9d577f69ac63e4d695 pedrom89.tib ``` ``` [jfa@fbsd /usr/local/share/tiemu/pedrom]$ sha256sum pedrom89.tib 4e04d4b53841aaf511934cf7a5fd4a9bb4603112f9b6fb9d577f69ac63e4d695 pedrom89.tib ``` On both Ubuntu and FBSD, the startup failure is exactly what I'm trying to fix. When the user first runs `tiemu` they get a startup wizard: Clicking "OK" starts the image import path, but TiEmu doesn't find any useable images, so the wizard popup just refreshes. Over and over. Looking into it, I could see that the validation/conversion path is failing for these included files. My hunch is that these files are malformed somehow, either missing the header or have the wrong header. I'm pretty confident that the import path is correct and functional. With the OS images in our PedroM package placed in `share/tiemu/pedrom/` you get this: And everything works. I've documented the function calls that constitute the validation path, if you're interested. So, my focus in setting it up this was is all about the user experience; this way, the user installs TiEmu and everything "just works". Of course, if you like to se it set up differently, we could just have the PedroM package only install the OS images, or put that mechanism in the `tiemu/build.sh` and just bundle the v0.83 images that way.

In the short term you can remove the `.git` from the SRCURL to fix the auto-update.
The problem is that it tries to use the SRCURL after the `git+` part as the API path and `OpenNMT/CTranslate2.git` is not a repo that exists.
We should probably strip `.git` from the end of git source URLs as part of the parsing in the auto-updater, but we don't usually put it at the end of git+ SRCURL's in the first place.

Well, by default, it does the following: It searches for the engine files in the parent directory, compiles and copies CTranslate2 files in the Python package folder, and exposes CTranslate2 bindings to Python. -DOPENMP_RUNTIME=NONE
-DCMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5
"
termux_step_pre_configure() {
	export CXXFLAGS+=" -I${TERMUX_PREFIX}/include/openblas -D_GNU_SOURCE"
	export LDFLAGS+=" -lc++_shared -landroid-posix-semaphore"
}
termux_step_post_make_install() {
	cd "$TERMUX_PKG_SRCDIR/python"
	export CTRANSLATE2_ROOT="$TERMUX_PREFIX"
	python -m build --wheel --no-isolation
	pip install dist/*.whl --no-deps --force-reinstall --prefix="$TERMUX_PREFIX"
	ln -sf "$TERMUX_PREFIX/lib/libctranslate2.so" \
		"$TERMUX_PYTHON_HOME/site-packages/ctranslate2/libctranslate2.so"
}
```

`python-ctranslate2.subpackage.sh`
```bash
TERMUX_SUBPKG_INCLUDE="
lib/python*/site-packages/ctranslate2/
lib/python*/site-packages/ctranslate2-*.dist-info/
"
TERMUX_SUBPKG_DESCRIPTION="Python bindings for CTranslate2"
TERMUX_SUBPKG_DEPENDS="python, python-numpy"
TERMUX_SUBPKG_PLATFORM_INDEPENDENT=false
```

This is my idea of what the final project will look like.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
> would it be possible to just make linting a separate workflow, just like the Auto update dry run workflow and the test-buildorder-random are, and would that fix this?

Possible yes, sensible I don't think so.
The linter step runs before build environment setup to conserve CI resources in case issues get flagged by the linter.
We could put it in a separate workflow, but that doesn't address the flagged problems and it wastes CI time on a package build that will need to be rerun to fix them anyways.
We could consider adding a commit trailer to the workflow, similar to `%ci:no-build` to skip the linter specifically.
But ignoring the linter mostly defeats its purpose.
It's there to make the build scripts more consistent.
If you think some linter warning is overzealous or imprecise then that should probably be addressed by a change to the linter instead of the workflow step.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
Regarding doing a patch apply test as part of linting in particular;
That's very messy since downloading and preparing the source directory involves running a significant chunk of the build system to get to the point where `termux_step_patch_package` is called.
That's significantly more complex than any of the existing linter checks and would take a relatively long time to run, even in a parallel workflow, compared to the current static analysis by the linter.
And it'd require non-trivial clean up to return the build directory to a clean slate afterwards.
I think letting patch problems be build failures is the most reasonable approach, though it is far more iterative.

A standalone `scripts/bin/check-patches` could be useful to test all patches against the build directory and provide a summary of all patch failures instead of seeing them one at a time over repeated build attempts as you fix them one by one.

payload.author: twaik
payload.body:
The pulseaudio half addresses more than one thing, and I think the "no measurable difference" case is worth spelling out.

`--no-as-needed,-lOpenSLES` fixes those reports by force-loading the platform `libOpenSLES.so` at exec time — and with it the entire platform dependency chain, a couple of hundred libraries, straight into the daemon's own namespace. That's namespace pollution in the other direction: platform copies of `libz.so`, `liblzma.so`, `libc++.so` and friends end up sitting next to the Termux ones, and whichever got there first wins for everything loaded afterwards. The pollution never went anywhere — pulseaudio just doesn't appear to reach a codepath where one of the mismatched symbols actually gets called. That's luck rather than correctness, and it depends on which modules a given user loads. Loading the library into a namespace of its own removes the whole class instead of trading one direction of it for the other.

On the fd limit, which is the part that showed no difference on that device: try lowering the limit there. With this change we're essentially opening a long list of libraries again, and pulseaudio caps itself at 256 open files — the linker needs an fd per library while loading a group, so it's easy to run past that and get something like `dlopen failed: library "libjpegencoder.so" not found` for a library that's sitting right there in `/system/lib64`. On mine: 256 fails, 384 works.

> do you have a device that is able to reproduce one of the problems with pulseaudio, or is the change entirely untested yet?

Not untested — I just didn't want it to depend on owning a broken device. I reproduced the collision deliberately instead: put an empty `liblzma.so` on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, and a direct `dlopen()` of the platform `libOpenSLES.so` then fails with `cannot locate symbol "Xzs_Construct"`, the same error as in the reports, while going through the wrapper still works. All three wrappers map the same set of platform libraries with and without that poisoned path. In that same poisoned environment pulseaudio still loads `module-sles-sink`, and audio drains in real time rather than being swallowed.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
Hi sorry for the delay on the review, I just got to this now. The build itself seems to run fine locally. But it looks like you updated your PR branch via `git merge`. Merge commits aren't supported by our package build workflows. Please make sure to update your branches with `git rebase`. I have rebased your branch manually from the PR interface to fix this for now.

You also seem to have used `master` as the branch for your PR, we generally recommend making a new "feature branch" for PRs to prevent problems from new commits to the upstream `master` branch while your PR is pending.

As an example for how you may wanna handle updating PRs in future cases, this is my general PR workflow.

#### Setup: As a one time setup after `git clone`-ing my development fork of termux-packages I add an `upstream` remote to the repository to pull new changes from. ```console git remote add upstream https://github.com/termux/termux-packages.git ``` #### Making a new PR branch. ```console # Switch to `master` for a clean slate git switch master # Create (`-c`) and then `switch` to a new branch. # e.g. forgejo-16.0.1 or whatever you wanna name your branch git switch -c forgejo-16.0.1 ``` Make your changes, make your commit(s), push your commit(s) you know the drill. #### Updating your branches with new changes from `upstream`. ```console # Fetch the `upstream` remote's `master` branch # And if that succeeded then take the (new) commits from `upstream/master` # and place them on top of `master`. git fetch -v upstream master && git rebase upstream/master master # (Optionally) push the updated `master` branch to your fork. git push # Switch back to your PR branch. git switch forgejo-16.0.1 # Rebase your branch against the updated `master` branch. git rebase master # Rebasing a branch with existing commits alters the history of that branch. # Thus you must force push the changes to overwrite the existing branch history. # --force-with-lease and --force-if-includes helps avoid mishaps due to this. git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes ``` You *may* have to resolve any merge conflicts that occur because of differing changes to the files that have been modified on your branch and changes made to those files in `upstream/master`[^1] since you branched off of `master`[^2]. [^1]: `upstream/master` is the `master` branch of `termux/termux-packages`. [^2]: `master`, or `origin/master` being the `master` branch of *your* fork of termux/termux-packages.

@MrStickyPiston by the way just so you understand fully, I think you should change your commit message to fix typos and also correct the explanation that has mistakes; here are my corrections so if you read my version of the text you can understand what you wrote that was wrong:


> This PR sets the cargo target for harper build.
Without setting the target, cargo would default to the host's target. For the termux github actions build system, this means all targets would build for GNU/Linux, as this is the host system operating system. This made all the packages unusable.


x64_86 is a typo of x86_64 that should be removed, but also, not only that but this doesn't have anything to do with architecture specifically - it has to do with the operating system, and because of that, the x86_64 build from `pkg install` actually does _not_ currently work on x86_64 Android devices, because it's for x86_64 GNU/Linux, not x86_64 Android, and x86_64 GNU/Linux compiled programs don't work on x86_64 Android, so it is incorrect to say "the non x64_86 packages are unusable" - actually all the packages are unusable until this is fixed.

Does that make sense to you?

payload.author: 3ls-it
payload.body:
> > I did experiment with CMake tweaks to the INDI build but had no luck. Admittedly they were somewhat superficial and it can be done, but once I was to the point where it looked like a lot more work than modifying the libnova install, I abandoned that path.
> 
> did you find the lines of code where the difference automatically occurs?

I played around with the `FindNova.cmake` module. I'm not confident that I know (yet) how to properly do that. And I did not yet ask my assistant to figure it out. In `cmake_modules/FindNova.cmake` we have this:  
```cmake
if (NOVA_INCLUDE_DIR AND NOVA_LIBRARIES)

  # in cache already
  set(NOVA_FOUND TRUE)
  message(STATUS "Found libnova: ${NOVA_LIBRARIES}")

else (NOVA_INCLUDE_DIR AND NOVA_LIBRARIES)

  find_path(NOVA_INCLUDE_DIR libnova/libnova.h
    PATH_SUFFIXES
    ${_obIncDir}
    ${GNUWIN32_DIR}/include
  )

  find_library(NOVA_LIBRARIES NAMES nova libnova libnovad
    PATHS
    ${_obLinkDir}
    ${GNUWIN32_DIR}/lib
  )
```  

And in `indi/build.sh` I set the cache with:
```sh
TERMUX_PKG_EXTRA_CONFIGURE_ARGS="
-DNOVA_INCLUDE_DIR=$TERMUX_PREFIX/include
"
```  
Well, it's amazing what a good night's sleep and a fresh pair of eyes can do! After pasting the above and thinking a little more about how the discovery works, I realised that I was missing something painfully simple and obvious. I edited `inidi/build.sh` thusly:  
```sh
TERMUX_PKG_EXTRA_CONFIGURE_ARGS="
-DNOVA_INCLUDE_DIR=$TERMUX_PREFIX/include
-DNOVA_LIBRARIES=$TERMUX_PREFIX/lib/libnova*
"
```  
and INDI compiles just fine with no library symlinks/modifications. It was that easy after all!! A little embarrassing really.  
```

payload.author: DevGitPit
payload.body:
@TomJo2000 so libskiasharp had the license check issue with ddc403826e9af224f78c832c76cad7a733756f45

---

Only explanation I got was- 

### 1. Bug 1: Multi-file `TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE_FILE` is broken upstream
In upstream `scripts/build/termux_step_install_license.sh`:
```bash
done <<< "${TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE_FILE//,/$'\n'}"
```
In `bash`, putting `$'\n'` inside double quotes (`"${.../$'\n'}"`) does **not** create a newline—it replaces commas with a space (`0x20`).

If a package defines multiple license files like:
```bash
TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE_FILE="LICENSE.txt, externals/skia/LICENSE"
```
Upstream reads it in one single line as `"LICENSE.txt externals/skia/LICENSE"`, and immediately fails with:
```
ERROR: .../LICENSE.txt externals/skia/LICENSE does not exist
```

---

### 2. Bug 2: Missing standard `LICENSE.md` and `LICENSE.txt`
Prior to commit `31e410cd99`, the list explicitly had:
```bash
'license.txt' 'License.txt' 'LICENSE.txt' 'LICENSE.TXT' 'license.md' 'LICENSE.md'
```
When refactored into loops, it added extensions (`.md`, `.txt`) **before** uppercasing:
```bash
# Adds .md/.txt to lowercase 'license' -> 'license.md'
COMMON_LICENSE_FILES+=("$LICENSE"{.md,.rst,.txt})

# @u capitalizes first letter -> 'License.md'
# @U capitalizes all letters  -> 'LICENSE.MD'
```
As a result, **`LICENSE.md`** and **`LICENSE.txt`** (capital name + lowercase extension, the GitHub defaults) were accidentally dropped from the search list.

---

### 3. Why `libskiasharp` needs both:
Even once the script's auto-detection is fixed:
* `libskiasharp` has its BSD 3-Clause license in `externals/skia/LICENSE` (a subdirectory).
* The build system never searches subdirectories automatically.
* Therefore, `libskiasharp` **must** define:
  ```bash
  TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE="MIT, BSD 3-Clause"
  TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE_FILE="LICENSE.txt, externals/skia/LICENSE"
  ```
* And parsing `TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE_FILE` with multiple files requires the fix in `termux_step_install_license.sh` so bash splits on commas correctly.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
I did actually have a new idea for the `neovim-nightly` problem.
Instead of parsing the HTML body of the release entry we should be able to check `git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/neovim/neovim nightly`.

We can find the nightly version with `git describe`
```console
~$ git describe --all
# tags/nightly
~$ git describe --first-parent
# v0.12.0-1049-gad3720b882
```
There's a bit of an edgecase here in that `nvim --version`[^1][^2] reports this as `v0.13.0-dev-1049+gad3720b882`, but that's a fairly easy to handle transformation.

And if we need to transform that output anyway then we may as well drop the sed expression and handle it in the function before passing the transformed result.

[^1]: https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/v0.12.4/.github/workflows/release.yml#L94-L99
[^2]: https://github.com/neovim/neovim/releases/tag/nightly

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
This *seems* to work since there's no way to "`git remote-describe`" a repo.
```bash
git clone https://github.com/neovim/neovim --filter=tree:0 --sparse
git -C neovim checkout nightly
git -C neovim describe --first-parent
```

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
@robertkirkman I have pushed the updated auto-update function for `neovim-nightly` to this branch now. This should hopefully be more reliable than the earlier approach of parsing the HTML body of the nightly release page. Although it does require additional transformation of the returned version string to match the format supplied by `nvim --version`.

As a sidenote, since our `neovim-nightly` package is built from a commit tarball it doesn't currently contain the part of the version info after `-dev`. So our `neovim-nightly`'s `nvim --version` reports `v0.13.0-dev` instead of `v0.13.0-dev-1095+g53cbf66bd2`, which would be the full version. I couldn't figure out a way for us to overwrite `-DNVIM_VERSION`[^1], it may be worth opening an issue with upstream to ask them to make it overwritable, or provide some other means for the build to determine its precise version from a tarball build. [^1]: https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/v0.12.4/cmake/GenerateVersion.cmake

payload.body:
Wow, every time it processes a step, it reads a log of the entire issue #29690 and everything we said in there and compares it with the current status of its test results, right? That is what this looks like it shows,

and I found that it shows this at some points:

> **The one incorrect assumption in the startup sequence:** LibreOffice assumes the loader merges all weak `type_info` copies to one address process-wide (true on glibc, the basis for UNO's whole cross-.so exception model). **Bionic doesn't** — it merges only within a dlopen group. So the startup closure and each dlopen'd UNO component end up with *different* `type_info` addresses for the same class, and since aarch64 libc++abi matches catches by pointer identity, every typed `catch` across that boundary silently fails.

> promote the startup closure into the global group before components load, so both sides resolve to the same canonical `type_info`.

> **Root cause chain:** Bionic resolves weak vague-linkage symbols per dlopen group (glibc interposes process-wide), so UNO exception `type_info` exists at different addresses in the exe startup closure vs. dlopen'd UNO components → libc++abi pointer-identity catch matching fails → typed catches miss, exceptions hit `catch(...)`/terminate. Fixes: 0028 (RTLD_GLOBAL on all component dlopens), 0040 (bridge Rtti uses RTLD_DEFAULT on Android), 0042 (promote startup closure to global group via dl_iterate_phdr + dlopen RTLD_NOLOAD|RTLD_GLOBAL at top of soffice_main). 0041 = RTTI-DIAG instrumentation in ShowBackingComponent's catch(...). Device readelf sweep (test-report.txt) proved: type_info WEAK DEFAULT locally defined in ~150 .so, single libc++_shared — not a visibility bug.


in summary, how I would rephrase this is, it appears that the weak symbols being `dlopen()`ed in some `.so` files of Libreoffice in the `abi.cxx` file are intended to access each others' symbols, but only glibc allows that, and for bionic libc, it is necessary to remove the `dlopen()` and also link all the symbols in libreoffice into the global group using `-Wl,-z,global`, at which point `RTLD_DEFAULT` in the `app_(RTLD_DEFAULT)` macro is able to access them.

payload.author: DevGitPit
payload.body:
I had to look as well. While I was trying to fix the build, I asked this to AI, and the answer is pasted- 

The `is { Count: > 0 }` syntax is a newer C# property pattern check (introduced in C# 9.0/10.0). Since the stable v4 branch was originally written to target older .NET environments and compiler versions, using the newer syntax in a backport runs the risk of compilation errors depending on the compiler version.

Additionally, `is { Count: > 0 }` requires the collection to explicitly have a `Count` property. The standard `!= null && Any()` check is a bulletproof, classic C# approach that works on **any** collection type (any `IEnumerable<T>`) and compiles successfully on any C# compiler version. It was chosen to ensure maximum compatibility and zero build-time risk.

PS- As for cherry-picking the commit that contains these changes is quite huge even if syntax was same. So yes syntax is different and that is also the reason for writing the patch file.

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
There are three packages in Termux that currently still have the Debian-like binary-header package split after https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/commit/6e70277fb3fe8e57114ecad786d92a4a2c7726f6 ,

One of them is `xorgproto`, and that split is enforced by the upstream developers through the way they distribute their code, and in both Arch Linux and Termux is now de facto attached unconditionally to `libx11` through dependency.

The other ones are `libglvnd-dev`, which was created in this PR:

- https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/pull/14696

and `mesa-dev`, which is also, like how I am making `qt5-qtbase` and `qt6-qtbase` now, marked as depending on `libglvnd-dev`, was created here:

- https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/pull/12852

Arch Linux's `libglvnd` and `mesa` are not split:

https://archlinux.org/packages/extra/x86_64/libglvnd/

https://archlinux.org/packages/extra/x86_64/mesa/

I don't think the original reason for the creation of `mesa-dev` involving `gst-plugins-base` is likely to still be reproducible, but at this point I don't really want to remove `libglvnd-dev` or `mesa-dev` without a really good reason to because I think it would confuse long-time Termux users and shuffle files around between packages kind of pointlessly.

For now, I think writing a big comment about this like this for future reference and discussion if needed and proceeding with following the precedent of `libx11` and `mesa-dev` of marking packages as depending on the header-only packages that contain headers that their own headers use `#include` on is sufficient.

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
Before this PR, the normal bootstrap (`.zip` format without aggressive compression tool, the same way they are built in the official Termux) is 31091622 bytes, and with this PR it is 32259142 bytes, which is approximately a 1 MiB increase,

however, I'd like to note something that might be relevant for consideration by others, which is that this PR would make building the package `aosp-libs` required during the use of `build-bootstraps.sh`,

as a maintainer of `aosp-libs` package I wouldn't personally necessarily mind having it built as a build dependency of the bootstrap, since logically purely from my perspective it would be a tradeoff which increases build time but also increases the amount of testing that the package would receive, ensuring that if it stops building we would be aware sooner,

but I also think that there's a high chance that the tradeoff would be seen as unfavorable from the perspective of some people, because the idea of hearing "to build Termux App from source, you need to download AOSP source code and compile a custom ROM that then needs to run in a weird emulator to compile a small part of one of the dependencies of one of the packages that is by default in Termux" might be uncomfortable for some people.

The reason this becomes necessary is because of the use of said weird emulator to specifically run the `asn1Parser` tool of `p11-kit` during its building in order to cross-compile (or _almost_ cross-compile?) `p11-kit` without encountering errors,

https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/blob/255c68bfda0dbe3d97722c60cae651808b3b5073/packages/p11-kit/0001-workaround-asn1Parser-for-cross-compile.diff#L24

One way that this concern could be entirely resolved, removing the build dependency on `aosp-libs`, is by implementing what could be called "full traditional cross-compilation", by creating a "host build" binary of the `asn1Parser` tool and using that instead, using the `g++` tool included with the Ubuntu image in the way that some packages such as `calligra` currently do:

https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/blob/255c68bfda0dbe3d97722c60cae651808b3b5073/x11-packages/calligra/build.sh#L20-L41

That isn't necessarily required in my opinion, that's just some general ideas about this PR from a couple of possible perspectives that come to mind that I imagine others might have.

`preconv`'s own `--version` message discloses this information.

GNU preconv (groff) version 1.25.0.rc1.57-653d0 with iconv support and with uchardet support
```
 
>     * Clarify what files we're installing from the host-build version.

There's been [some discussion along those lines this month](https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/groff/2026-07/msg00042.html) on the _groff_ mailing list.  Apparently some distributors who build for multiple architectures (or ABIs) want to minimize the time spent building, and the documentary build artifacts that a _groff_ build generates (such as its own manuals, apart from the GNU-mandated Texinfo one) are supposed to be byte-identical (if `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` is used) regardless of what the platform's ISA, integer endianness, and so forth are.

...
>       * URW fonts, aside from being poorly documented are also seemingly a nightmare to get working with cross-builds.

They're a nightmare to get working in a native build, too.  Every time a _groff_ release goes into release candidate, Deri James (@derij) and I fight our way through a fresh crop of issues.

>         The directory search list for determining if URW fonts are supported/available is hardcoded in the `configure` script.
>         We have them in `ghostscript`, and we could use it as a build dependency (and I'm guessing optional runtime dependency, although I have not checked that relation), but the configure script won't search our ghostscript fonts directory for them so URW fonts never get detected for cross-builds.

Deri recently pointed out that URW fonts that ship in "ghostscript" directories are inadequate for _gropdf_'s "full service level", because the AFM files--the font metrics--are not present. ([thread](https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/groff/2026-07/msg00066.html))
 
>         I suspect this is at least partly why we're copying the devpdf fonts from the host-build.
>       * URW font detection on the host-build is also a nightmare.
>         Since the search list is hardcoded it's also gonna fail for on-device builds or _weird_ host systems.

I'd advise _any_ distributor to decide whether they want _gropdf_'s "full service level", and if they do, to _always_ specify `--with-urw-fonts=$wherever` to _groff_'s configure script. payload.author: glebm

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
I see, well if you prefer not to have that, then you can remove the comment; what would be enough is to just add the second commit that adds `devilutionx` in the same PR here.

The reason I think it is best to organize it that way is to make it clear what the purpose of the package being added originally was, so that in the future, let's say for example 2 years from now the `google-benchmark` package stops working or fails to build, and people at that time wonder "why is this needed and could we disable or remove it without ruining someone's workflow?" then they could associate it with `devilutionx` in that context, and check whether the package `devilutionx` is still being updated at that time or not, and if so then the people of the future wouldn't want to remove `google-benchmark`.

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body: I guess it might be relevant for me to say, that Termux developers often operate in a decentralized and very loosely organized way, and I have observed other Termux developers periodically enforcing the "no libraries without reverse dependencies" rule by going through the repository and removing library packages that are orphaned, outdated or lacking sufficient reverse dependencies. This context hopefully provides a clearer picture of why I am thinking this way about `google-benchmark`.

in Termux, it is not recommended to set a versioned dependency in `apt`, but it is possible as a last resort or necessary in some specific cases. The specific cases where versioned dependencies are required in Termux `apt` are significantly fewer than those in Debian and are much more comparable to those in Arch Linux. The default behavior is for the dependency to not be marked as versioned in `apt`, so currently, 

to answer your question fully, yes by default dependencies upgrade regardless of consumer package state.

payload.author: therealviren
payload.body:
Thank you for the response. I understand the packaging policy. However, I’d like to clarify that this is a fully functional text editor project and not a personal or experimental repository.
If possible, I would appreciate it if you could take another look at the project to evaluate it against the packaging criteria.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
> However, I’d like to clarify that this is a fully functional text editor project and not a personal or experimental repository.

That doesn't clear the bar for our packaging policy unfortunately.

> If possible, I would appreciate it if you could take another look at the project to evaluate it against the packaging criteria. I understand if it still does not fit the scope of the official Termux packages. Thank you for your time and consideration.

I have included the checklist from our package request issue template below as I would evaluate it for this package-

### Packaging policy acknowledgement
<!-- Fill out as appropriate for PR -->
- [x] The project is actively developed.
- [ ] The project has [existing packages](https://repology.org/projects/) and is "well known".
- [x] Licensed under an [open source license](https://spdx.org/licenses/).
- [ ] Not available through a language package manager: pip, npm, cpan, cargo, etc.
*Marking as not met, this point is a bit imprecisely worded.
Termux is a supported installation target in the `install.sh`.
`git clone` + `cd` + `./install.sh` is a reasonably low friction way to install the project.*
- [x] Not taking up too much disk space (< 100MiB per architecture, exceptions can be made)
- [~] Not duplicating the functionality of existing packages.
- [x] Not serving hacking, malware, phishing, spamming, spying, ddos functionality.
- [x] I certify that I have read [Termux Packaging Policy](https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#packaging-policy) and understand that my request will be denied if it is found lacking.

The points that aren't met here aren't huge dealbreakers over all.
But the specific combination of:
- New project (and thus no existing userbase)
- Easily installable by a user without an overly complex build process.
- In a package category that is very well served by [existing packages](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Atermux%2Ftermux-packages+bin%2Feditor+language%3ARAML&type=code&l=RAML).

Leads me towards a no when it comes to packaging.
Any package we offer in the repositories requires space, bandwidth and ongoing maintenance.
Thus we would like to ensure that any packages we choose to add to the repositories meet a baseline for utility to users.
That is not meant to discourage your package in any way, we simply have a chicken and egg problem here.

payload.author: FuPeiJiang
payload.body:
I kept the custom `termux_step_configure()`, `termux_step_make()`, and `termux_step_make_install()` for now because switching fully to `android-build-tools`' CMake install path appears to change the package contents.

`android-build-tools` does define CMake targets for the internal Android libraries, but they are static CMake targets. Its install rule only installs the tools:

- `aidl`
- `aapt`
- `aapt2`
- `zipalign`

It does not install the shared libraries currently shipped by Termux's `aapt` package, such as `libandroid-base.so`, `libandroid-fw.so`, `libandroid-utils.so`, etc. The current Termux recipe still installs those shared libraries in `packages/aapt/build.sh`, and `packages/sysprop/build.sh` explicitly notes that it depends on `aapt` for `libandroid-base.so`.

So removing the custom make/install steps may be the right direction, but it is not just a cleanup. It likely changes the package ABI/files provided and may require moving those libraries elsewhere or updating reverse dependencies.

I also kept `termux_step_make_install()` because it creates `$PREFIX/share/aapt/android.jar` from the Android 36 platform jar, which is needed by `aapt2 link`.

The no-op `termux_step_configure()` is only there because the recipe is still using the existing manual build path. If it is removed, the default Termux configure step sees `CMakeLists.txt` and attempts to configure the upstream CMake project. That should be tested together with removing the manual `termux_step_make()` / `termux_step_make_install()` path.

The symlink loop is kept because `android-build-tools` stores the AOSP sources under `vendor/...`, while the existing Termux patches and manual build expect top-level paths such as `base`, `aidl`, `core`, `libbase`, etc. Since `termux_step_post_get_source()` runs before patch application, those symlinks are currently needed both for patch paths and for the manual build variables.

The previous custom `termux_step_get_source()` was mainly for pinning the exact `android-build-tools` commit, and it also contained the now-removed submodule URL overrides. I removed that custom source step. The recipe now uses the default Termux git source handling and verifies the checked-out commit in `termux_step_post_get_source()`, so if `android-build-tools` `master` moves, the build fails instead of silently building a different revision.

payload.author: FuPeiJiang
payload.body:
I reproduced the same `F Vector` message locally with `aapt` from a host CMake build. I do not think CMake itself is the root cause; the relevant difference is the assert/logging configuration used by the host build.

The reproducing command was a normal minimal `aapt package` command:

```sh
aapt package \
  -f \
  -M /tmp/aapt-debug/AndroidManifest.xml \
  -S /tmp/aapt-debug/res \
  -I /path/to/Android/Sdk/platforms/android-36/android.jar \
  -F /tmp/aapt-debug/out.apk
```

The input was a minimal manifest using `targetSdkVersion="36"` plus one `res/values/strings.xml`. I also tried a more realistic manifest label using `@string/app_name`, adding `-J`, and adding explicit `--min-sdk-version 24 --target-sdk-version 36`; those did not change the result. So I do not think this is caused by a missing important `aapt` argument.

For the diagnostic build, I used an assertion-enabled build while keeping verbose logs disabled:

```sh
cat > /tmp/aapt-debug-log-overrides.h <<'EOF2'
#pragma once
#define LOG_NDEBUG 0
#define ALOGV(...) do { } while (0)
#define ALOGV_IF(cond, ...) do { } while (0)
EOF2

cmake -S /path/to/android-build-tools \
  -B /tmp/android-build-tools-host-aapt-assert-only \
  -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  "-DCMAKE_C_FLAGS_DEBUG=-g -O0 -include /tmp/aapt-debug-log-overrides.h" \
  "-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG=-g -O0 -include /tmp/aapt-debug-log-overrides.h"

cmake --build /tmp/android-build-tools-host-aapt-assert-only --target aapt -j "$(nproc)"
```

I used `LOG_NDEBUG=0` so Android fatal assertions stay enabled, but kept `ALOGV` disabled because enabling verbose logging also exercises unrelated debug-only paths.

The backtrace for the `F Vector` abort was:

```text
VectorImpl::itemLocation(index=0)
VectorImpl::_grow(where=0, amount=0)
VectorImpl::insertAt(..., numItems=0)
android::Vector<bool>::insertAt(false, 0, 0)
ResourceTable::flatten(...) at ResourceTable.cpp:3079
```

That points to:

```cpp
validResources.insertAt(false, 0, N);
```

where `N == 0`.

`N` here is:

```cpp
const size_t N = t->getOrderedConfigs().size();
```

`t` is a `ResourceTable::Type`, such as `attr`, `string`, `drawable`, `layout`, etc. Despite the name `getOrderedConfigs()`, this vector is effectively the ordered list of resource entries for that type. Each item is a `ConfigList`, meaning one resource name with possibly multiple configuration variants.

For example:

```xml
<string name="app_name">App</string>
```

makes `N == 1` for the `string` type.

If the same resource exists in multiple configurations:

```text
res/values/strings.xml       -> app_name
res/values-fr/strings.xml    -> app_name
```

`N` is still `1` for `string`; that one `ConfigList` contains multiple config entries.

In the reproducer, the failing type was `attr`:

```text
typeName = "attr"
N = 0
```

That happens because `ResourceTable` always creates the `attr` type up front:

```cpp
// Every resource table always has one first entry, the bag attributes.
getType(mAssetsPackage, String16("attr"), unknown);
```

A normal small app often defines no custom attrs, so the `attr` type exists but has no entries. Then this call becomes:

```cpp
validResources.insertAt(false, 0, 0);
```

and an assertion-enabled build aborts with:

```text
F Vector  : [...] itemLocation: index=0, capacity=0, count=0
```

I confirmed this by adding a real custom attribute:

```xml
<resources>
    <attr name="exampleAttr" format="string" />
</resources>
```

Conventionally that would go in `res/values/attrs.xml`, although any `res/values/*.xml` file is valid. With that attr present, the `attr` type has `N == 1`, and the same assertion-enabled `aapt package` command succeeds.

So my read is that this is an assertion-enabled build exposing a zero-length `Vector::insertAt()` path. In a release-style build the assertion is stripped and the command continues. A surgical fix would be to guard the caller:

```cpp
if (N > 0) {
    validResources.insertAt(false, 0, N);
}
```

or to make `VectorI

payload.author: FuPeiJiang
payload.body:
I rechecked this and need to correct/clarify my earlier CMake wording: the default CMake build is involved, because `NDEBUG` is applied inconsistently across targets.

`vendor/libandroidfw.cmake` has:

```cmake
target_compile_definitions(libandroidfw PUBLIC
    NDEBUG
    STATIC_ANDROIDFW_FOR_TOOLS
)
```

That propagates to consumers of `libandroidfw`, such as `libaapt`, so `ResourceTable.cpp` is compiled with `-DNDEBUG`. It does not propagate backward into dependencies of `libandroidfw`, such as `libutils`. In the default CMake build I checked, the relevant shape is:

```text
ResourceTable.cpp: built with -DNDEBUG
VectorImpl.cpp:   built without -DNDEBUG
```

The abort happens in `VectorImpl.cpp`, so `libutils` still has the fatal assertion active:

```text
F Vector  : [...] itemLocation: index=0, capacity=0, count=0
```

The source path is still the same latent zero-length insert:

```cpp
const size_t N = t != NULL ? t->getOrderedConfigs().size() : 0;
...
validResources.insertAt(false, 0, N);
```

Current AOSP main:
https://android.googlesource.com/platform/frameworks/base/+/refs/heads/main/tools/aapt/ResourceTable.cpp#3079

Exact `frameworks/base` commit used by the current `android-build-tools` submodule:
https://android.googlesource.com/platform/frameworks/base/+/45034f0663f960d9ee5fb0a101a4732b71f6e2f4/tools/aapt/ResourceTable.cpp#3079

In my repro, `N == 0` because the current type was `attr`. `ResourceTable` creates the `attr` type up front so it is first:

```cpp
// Every resource table always has one first entry, the bag attributes.
getType(mAssetsPackage, String16("attr"), unknown);
```

A small app can define no custom attrs, so the `attr` type exists but has no entries. If I add a custom attr, conventionally in `res/values/attrs.xml`:

```xml
<resources>
    <attr name="exampleAttr" format="string" />
</resources>
```

then `N == 1` for `attr`, and this specific abort goes away.

I locally tested the CMake-side fix. The working version is to add `NDEBUG` to `libutils`, but keep `ANDROID_UTILS_REF_BASE_DISABLE_IMPLICIT_CONSTRUCTION` private:

```cmake
target_compile_definitions(libutils PUBLIC
    NDEBUG
)

target_compile_definitions(libutils PRIVATE
    ANDROID_UTILS_REF_BASE_DISABLE_IMPLICIT_CONSTRUCTION
)
```

With that change:

```text
VectorImpl.cpp:   built with -DNDEBUG
ResourceTable.cpp: built with -DNDEBUG
```

and the minimal `aapt package` command that previously aborted succeeds and produces the APK.

Fixes I did not take:

1. I did not make the whole existing `libutils` definition block `PUBLIC`:

```cmake
target_compile_definitions(libutils PUBLIC
    NDEBUG
    ANDROID_UTILS_REF_BASE_DISABLE_IMPLICIT_CONSTRUCTION
)
```

That fails to compile because `ANDROID_UTILS_REF_BASE_DISABLE_IMPLICIT_CONSTRUCTION` leaks into `aapt` and breaks legacy `sp<T> x = new T(...)` code.

2. I did not patch `aapt` with a caller guard:

```cpp
if (N > 0) {
    validResources.insertAt(false, 0, N);
}
```

That is a reasonable defensive source-level fix, but it is separate from the CMake build-mode inconsistency.

3. I did not patch `VectorImpl::insertAt(..., numItems=0)` to be a no-op. That would be the broadest source-level fix, but it touches shared Android utility code and has a larger blast radius.

So for the immediate CMake build failure, the narrow tested fix is: add `NDEBUG` publicly to `libutils`, while keeping the refbase construction guard private.

payload.author: FuPeiJiang
payload.body:
I rechecked this after your comment, and I think this is the right framing now.

The upstream `Android.bp` files do not need to mention `NDEBUG` because Soong applies it globally. In Soong's `cc/config/global.go`, `commonGlobalCflags` includes:

```text
-DANDROID
-DNDEBUG
-UDEBUG
```

and C/C++ modules receive those through `${config.CommonGlobalCflags}`. So the official build system's workaround/behavior is not in `aapt/Android.bp`, `libandroidfw/Android.bp`, or `libutils/Android.bp`; it is in Soong's global native flags.

That means the CMake port should translate this globally too, instead of adding `NDEBUG` target by target. I updated the android-build-tools PR accordingly:

https://github.com/termux/android-build-tools/pull/3

The PR now does this at the top level:

```cmake
add_compile_definitions(ANDROID NDEBUG)
add_compile_options($<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:C,CXX>:-UDEBUG>)
```

and removes the ad hoc `NDEBUG` from `vendor/libandroidfw.cmake`.

I built this before updating/commenting:

- default CMake host build of the full target set succeeded
- `VectorImpl.cpp` compile line now has `-DANDROID`, `-DNDEBUG`, and `-UDEBUG`
- `ResourceTable.cpp` compile line also has `-DANDROID`, `-DNDEBUG`, and `-UDEBUG`
- the minimal `aapt package` command against `android-36/android.jar` succeeds and produces an APK

On the assertion-enabled question: if the relevant upstream code is deliberately built with assertions enabled, for example with something like:

```text
-UNDEBUG
-DLOG_NDEBUG=0
```

then I would still expect this same source path to abort, because the zero-length insert is still present upstream:

```cpp
validResources.insertAt(false, 0, N);
```

with `N == 0` for the pre-created empty `attr` type. But that is not the normal official Soong build configuration. Normal Soong native builds get `-DNDEBUG -UDEBUG` globally, so this assertion is compiled out.

So the CMake fix is not trying to hide a CMake-only source bug. It is making CMake match Soong's global native build flags. The source-level defensive fix, if desired separately, would still be something like guarding the zero-length insert, but that is a different question from matching the official build behavior.

payload.title: fix(x11/flameshot): force-reenable X11 support in version 14

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
If upstream's replies are to be believed and interpreted literally as written, support for X11 might de facto disappear from a future version of Flameshot because upstream "has no long term support plan" for the case when xdg-desktop-portal does not work which is effectively always. at that time, Termux will no longer be able to receive upgrades to Flameshot until a maintained fork of Flameshot appears with restored X11 support.

I am maintaining a fork of Flameshot 12 for my personal use on Desktop Linux but I don't plan to rename it, release it with tags, or offer support for its use in non-Gentoo-based distros, so Termux packages will need to use some other fork that would have to be maintained by someone who is dedicated entirely to specifically maintaining a Flameshot fork.

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
Oh, well I (and you) forgot to apply the necessary code to force reenable the X11 compatibility of Flameshot which upstream has disabled:

- https://github.com/flameshot-org/flameshot/issues/4693

also, all Qt6-based versions of Flameshot, including both 13 and 14 are not correctly compatible with multi-monitor X11 configurations. however, for Termux:X11, this will not matter because Termux:X11 does not support multi-monitor, so there will be no measurable problem with Flameshot in Termux:X11 other than the necessary patch for version 14.

because I observed that, in what seems like 99% of cases, whether a package name begins with `kf6-` or not in Termux depends on whether that software packaged in Fedora has a name beginning with `kf6-` or not, meaning that to my observation, Termux seemed to "follow" the Fedora naming scheme, possibly, I assumed, because the person who originally named some of the KDE frameworks 6 packages in Termux was a user of Fedora and looked only at their own distro's repo when designing Termux's KDE frameworks 6 packages - so I thought that to preserve consistency, Fedora's choices might be relevant to the best choices Termux should choose for naming consistency.

Note that while Debian has source packages named beginning with `kf6-`, they usually choose different names for the binary packages from those source packages that don't begin with `kf6-`, making Debian's naming scheme differ from Termux's in a way in this case that Fedora's does not.

def hard_reset_via_esp(ip):
"""toggle GPIO12 via esp-link rest api."""
try:
url = f"http://{ip}/console/reset"
req = urllib.request.Request(url, method='POST')
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=2) as response:
if response.status == 200:
time.sleep(1) # Wait for STM32 to boot into loader
return True
except:
pass
return False

def get_checksum(data):
res = 0
for b in data: res ^= b
return res

def send_command(ser, cmd):
ser.write(bytes([cmd, cmd ^ 0xFF]))
res = ser.read(1)
return res == b'\x79'

def sync_stm32(ser):
"""Sends 0x7F and handles potential network garbage."""
ser.reset_input_buffer()
for _ in range(15):
ser.write(b'\x7f')
res = ser.read(1)
if res in [b'\x79', b'\x1f']:
return True
time.sleep(0.1)
return False

def run_flash():
try:
# Load binary early to catch file errors
with open(bnry_pth, "rb") as f:
content = f.read()

ser = None
synced = False

# retry cycle for sync
for attempt in range(1, 4):
print(f"[attempt {attempt}/3] resetting STM32 via GPIO12...")
hard_reset_via_esp(IP)

if ser: ser.close()
ser = serial.serial_for_url(f"socket://{IP}:{port_num}", timeout=2, parity='E')

print("syncing...")
if sync_stm32(ser):
synced = True
print("synced.")
break
else:
print("sync failed, retrying reset...")

if not synced:
print("\n failed to sync after 3 attempts.")
print("check: BOOT0 jumper = 1")
return

print("\n getting bootloader Info..")
if send_command(ser, 0x00):
n_raw = ser.read(1)
if n_raw:
num_bytes = ord(n_raw)
data = ser.read(num_bytes + 1)
ser.read(1)
version = data[0]
supported_cmds = list(data[1:])
print(f"• version: {version >> 4}.{version & 0xF}")
print(f"• supported commands: {['0x%02X' % c for c in supported_cmds]}")

# 2. GET CHIP ID (PID) (Command 0x02)
if send_command(ser, 0x02):
n_raw = ser.read(1)
if n_raw:
num_bytes = ord(n_raw) + 1
pid_bytes = ser.read(num_bytes)
ser.read(1) # Final ACK
chip_id = int.from_bytes(pid_bytes, 'big')
print(f"connected to chip PID: 0x{chip_id:03X}")
else:
print("chip protected. Unlocking...")
if send_command(ser, 0x92):
print("Unlocked. Re-syncing...")
time.sleep(2)
sync_stm32(ser)

# --- multiple choice options ---
print("choice the option:")
print(" [1] flashing (Erase + Write + Start)")
print(" [2] go(start executing the run the flash file)")
print(" [3] cancel (abort)")

choice = input("Select option (1/2/3): ").strip().lower()

if choice in ['3', 'no']:
print("operation cancalled.")
return

if choice in ['1', 'flash']:

print("\nerasing...")
if send_command(ser, 0x43):
ser.write(b'\xff\x00')
ser.read(1)
print("erased success.")

print(f"writing {len(content)} bytes...")
for i in range(0, len(content), 256):
chunk = content[i:i+256]
curr_addr = strng_add + i

if not send_command(ser, 0x31): break

addr_bytes = curr_addr.to_bytes(4, 'big')
ser.write(addr_bytes + bytes([get_checksum(addr_bytes)]))
if ser.read(1) != b'\x79': break

d_len = len(chunk) - 1
ser.write(bytes([d_len]) + chunk + bytes([d_len ^ get_checksum(chunk)]))
if ser.read(1) != b'\x79': break
print(f"progress: {i + len(chunk)}/{len(content)} bytes", end='\r')

print("\nFLASH SUCCESSFUL!")

# (executed for flash or go)
if choice in ['1', '2', 'flash', 'go']:
print("starting the program...")
if send_command(ser, 0x21):
addr_bytes = strng_add.to_bytes(4, 'big')
ser

payload.title: fix(main/zsh): do not load completions in etc/zshrc, causes delay

payload.author: robertkirkman
payload.body:
I think referencing other linux distros' examples for this decision is a good idea,
so far i've checked two, Arch Linux and OpenSUSE

Arch Linux doesn't appear to enable the completions,

OpenSUSE has something more interesting, which might be worth researching more or considering:

https://build.opensuse.org/projects/shells/packages/zsh/files/zshrc

I can't link directly to the line or don't know how to in OpenSUSE official repositories, so as a heads up, you'll need to read past the first few lines to be able to find it.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
OpenSuSE's etc/zshrc is definitely a lot more involved.
But I don't think it's a good fit for what we're going for.
We don't set up any aliases or shell options for example.

Arch's approach being the other extreme here, they do nothing for system zshrc and only load `etc/profile` via the zprofile.

We're about in the middle here.
We set up `command-not-found` and `PS1` passthrough.
And we load `etc/profile` from `zprofile`, but I don't think doing the whole alias and basic completions setup that SuSE does makes all that much sense for us.

payload.author: TomJo2000
payload.body:
Eh, to elaborate the "not a good fit for our needs" point from above.
Since we are more performance constrained on a phone than a typical desktop distro would be on their hardware I think it's more prudent for us to keep the system shell configs rather sparse as to not impact startup times for shells too much.

Further configuration is almost definitionally a matter of personal preference.
So leaving it to the user to configure seems most appropriate.
Not having completions enabled out of the box on Zsh still bothers me personally,
but if it's gonna cause such a severe startup delay then I think it's best to leave loading the completions to the user.

payload.author: agnostic-apollo
